This section is intended to collect literature reviews and critical summaries of research relevant to the site's main topics. At present, the individual review pages are still incomplete. They should be read as topic stubs and source collections rather than finished review essays.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Current status

Each review page below is still a stub. The pages currently function as placeholders for future literature summaries, source curation, and critique.
:::

## Current Review Topics

- [Interaction Forces in the Golf Swing](research-review-interaction-forces.html): stub page collecting material around Carol Putnam's work on interaction forces and segment sequencing.
- [Induced Acceleration Analysis](research-review-induced-acceleration-analysis.html): stub page for literature on force-contribution and acceleration-decomposition methods.
- [Baseball Pitching Biomechanics](research-review-baseball-pitching.html): stub page for cross-sport comparison material relevant to multi-segment throwing motions.
- [Shaft Flexibility in Golf Swing Dynamics](research-review-shaft-flexibility.html): stub page collecting literature on shaft bending, stiffness, and modeling assumptions.

## Editorial Intent

When these pages are completed, each review should do four things:

1. State the main question addressed in the literature.
2. Distinguish empirical findings from modeling assumptions and interpretation.
3. Explain what the cited work actually supports, and what it does not support.
4. Note where the literature bears directly on AffineDrift's claims and where it does not.

## Suggested Completion Order

1. [Induced Acceleration Analysis](research-review-induced-acceleration-analysis.html), because it is most directly relevant to force-attribution questions.
2. [Interaction Forces in the Golf Swing](research-review-interaction-forces.html), because it speaks to segment sequencing and passive/active interaction terms.
3. [Shaft Flexibility in Golf Swing Dynamics](research-review-shaft-flexibility.html), because shaft-model assumptions affect several golf-specific pages.
4. [Baseball Pitching Biomechanics](research-review-baseball-pitching.html), because it is useful mainly as a comparison domain rather than a direct golf source.
